paras: The attempted lynching of Leander Huff took place on July 28, 1888, at Concordia Landing, Mississippi, after Huff, mate of the steamer Coahoma, shot and killed a Black roustabout and a crowd of Black men demanded that he be handed over to be hanged. Huff fled across the river pursued by men in skiffs and turned up alive in Memphis on August 3. Papers retold his flight as "A Race for Life"; he was arrested in Memphis as a fugitive from justice in December.

Early on Saturday, July 28, the Coahoma lay at Concordia loading cotton seed. Walter Jackson, a Black eyewitness, told the Memphis Appeal that the mate often quarreled with one slow roustabout, "an unknown colored rouster," and had twice beaten him.

Jackson said that Huff knocked the man down and beat him, chased him off the boat, struck at him with a stick and shot him three times. A Memphis special in the Richmond Dispatch said instead that the man drew a knife and ripped Huff's sleeve before Huff fired, and the Memphis wire said he was shot "while attempting to cut the mate."

Black men from the landing and adjoining plantations gathered at the boat. The Dispatch wrote that about twenty demanded Huff "to be swung up" and threatened to burn the boat, and the Osceola Times said they were kept from burning it only "with the greatest difficulty." A crewman rowed Huff to an island near the Arkansas shore, skiffs of Black men followed, and the Dispatch doubted that he had escaped.

In his own account, reprinted from the St. Louis Republic, Huff said the crowd rushed the boat yelling "Kill him," a hatchet clipped his ear as he pushed off, and pursuers fired at him before he hid in the island's marsh grass. He said he swam to Arkansas, heard from a white fisherman that armed Black men patrolled the levee, and escaped on a log to a passing boat. The Louisville Courier-Journal's version had the Coahoma pick him up on its return trip.

In Memphis the boat's officers raised $200 and bought Huff a ticket east; he said he would return in the fall to stand trial. On December 30 a Memphis patrolman arrested him as a fugitive from justice; he had been living as Charles Howard. No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The first reports treated the event as a mate's killing of a deck hand: "Killed a Roustabout" in the Appeal, "Negro Killed by a Steamboat Mate" in the Indianapolis Journal. That Memphis wire, which said the mate fled "fearing violence at the hands of the negroes, who are largely in the majority at Concordia," also ran in the St. Paul Daily Globe and Ohio Democrat. Shorter items in the Springfield Daily Republic and Mississippi papers kept only the killing.

The Memphis special turned to the mate's danger, appearing in the Richmond Dispatch as "A Race for Life" with the line "Hunted by a Crowd of Vengeance-Seeking Negroes." After Huff reappeared, the Courier-Journal headed his story "Escaped from the Mob," and the New York Sun ran it on August 12 as "Hunted by Negroes Bent Upon Killing Him," after a German version in Baltimore's Der Deutsche Correspondent. These stories rested on Huff's telling and quoted his thought: "Better drown than be killed by these black devils." At his arrest the Appeal called him "A Murderer Captured" but again stressed his escape from "the Fury of a Mob of Negroes."

On who struck first, Jackson said Huff beat the man and shot him as he fled, the wire said the man came at Huff with a knife, and Huff told the Appeal in December that he first hit the man with a stick. The December report also named the boat as the Kate Adams, and the Courier-Journal placed the shooting at Carson's Landing.

In December Huff said the crowd at Concordia was dispersed, about twelve men followed him at the next landing, and he held them off with a pistol on Island Seventy-one until whites rescued him. The hatchet blow and shots appear only in the St. Louis Republic version and its German translation.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Leander Huff
bases: After Huff shot a Black roustabout, a crowd of Black men demanded him 'to be swung up', threatened to burn the boat and pursued him by skiff, but he escaped (A4, A6, A14, A15); the killing of the roustabout was by Huff alone.

A crowd of about twenty (A4) or a dozen (A15) men without legal authority sought to hang Huff for killing the roustabout, but he escaped alive (A8, A14, A15); the one death, the roustabout's, was a shooting by one man, not a group.

The killing and the crowd's threats against Huff appear in separate Memphis reports (A1, A2, A4), an independent Arkansas brief (A6) and Huff's own later accounts (A14, A15), though details of the pursuit differ.

accounts.label: Black eyewitness (Walter Jackson)
accounts.gist: Huff, angry at a slow worker he had beaten before, knocked him down and beat him, chased him off the boat, struck at him with a stick and shot him three times; Huff escaped.

accounts.label: Memphis wire
accounts.gist: The deck hand was shot three times while attempting to cut the mate; fearing violence from the negroes, the mate was rowed to the Arkansas side.

accounts.label: Memphis special
accounts.gist: The roustabout drew a knife; about twenty negroes demanded Huff be handed over to be hanged and threatened to burn the boat; skiffs pursued him to an island and his escape was doubtful.

accounts.label: Huff's account (St. Louis Republic, Aug. 3)
accounts.gist: A crowd rushed the boat yelling 'Kill him', clipped his ear with a hatchet, chased him by skiff and fired at him; he hid for days in swamps, swam to Arkansas and escaped on a log to a passing boat.

accounts.label: Huff's account (Courier-Journal, Aug. 3)
accounts.gist: Pursued closely, he hid in cane while two or three men searched the island, swam to the Arkansas shore and traveled upriver until the Coahoma picked him up.

accounts.label: Huff's account after arrest (December)
accounts.gist: He hit the man with a stick, then shot him when he attacked with a knife; the crowd threatened to hang him but was dispersed; at the next landing about twelve men followed him, he swam to Island Seventy-one, held them off with a pistol and was rescued by whites.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal's first report, 'Killed a Roustabout', gave a Black eyewitness's account unfavorable to the mate.
The Memphis wire ('Negro Killed by a Steamboat Mate') presented the shooting as self-defense against a knife and the 'negroes' majority at Concordia as the danger.
The Richmond Dispatch's 'A Race for Life. Hunted by a Crowd of Vengeance-Seeking Negroes' cast the mate as the hunted party.
The Courier-Journal ('Escaped from the Mob ... Blood-Thirsty Negroes') and the Sun ('Hunted by Negroes Bent Upon Killing Him') told Huff's escape as an adventure in his own words.
The Appeal's December headline 'A Murderer Captured' paired with the subhead that he escaped 'the Fury of a Mob of Negroes.'
